_about: FINAL test set (2026-10-24): 42 answers on 7 new fictional projects, Claude-authored labels on the 0-4 rubric, fixed before any evaluator ran. Answer length deliberately varied within each tier (concise strong answers, long weak ones). Run ONCE for the reported numbers; never tune on it.

medremind.title: MedRemind - Medication Reminder App
medremind.summary: React Native app that reminds elderly users to take medicines; local notifications scheduled per dose, caregiver alerts via Firebase Cloud Messaging when a dose is missed, offline storage with AsyncStorage.

libsearch.title: LibSearch - College Library Search Engine
libsearch.summary: Search engine over 40,000 library catalogue records using Elasticsearch with a Flask API; fuzzy matching for misspelled titles and author-name boosting; React front end.

fleetwatch.title: FleetWatch - Delivery Fleet Tracker
fleetwatch.summary: Real-time tracking for a 30-vehicle delivery fleet: drivers' phones send GPS every 10 seconds over WebSockets to a Go service; positions stored in PostGIS; geofence alerts when a vehicle leaves its zone.

examproctor.title: Internship - QA Automation Intern at ExamPro
examproctor.summary: QA automation intern (June-August 2025) at an online exam platform; wrote Selenium and Pytest end-to-end tests for the exam-taking flow and ran them in GitHub Actions.

plantdoc.title: PlantDoc - Leaf Disease Classifier
plantdoc.summary: Classifies 12 tomato leaf diseases from phone photos using transfer learning on MobileNetV2 in TensorFlow, converted to TensorFlow Lite for an Android app; 94% validation accuracy.

splitledger.title: SplitLedger - Hostel Expense Ledger (Team of 4)
splitledger.summary: Web app for hostel roommates to log shared expenses; Node.js and Express API, MySQL database, settle-up calculation, monthly PDF statements. Built by a team of four.

chatsupport.title: HelpBot - RAG Support Chatbot
chatsupport.summary: Customer-support chatbot for a college IT helpdesk: answers from 300 help articles using retrieval-augmented generation with FAISS and sentence-transformer embeddings, Llama 3 8B via an API, with source links in every answer.

items.question: How does MedRemind make sure a reminder still fires if the phone is offline?

answers.why: Correct: local scheduled notifications need no network; what does need it; concrete handling.
answers.answer: Reminders are local notifications scheduled on the phone when a dose is saved, so they fire with no network. Only the caregiver alert needs internet: if a dose isn't marked taken within 30 minutes, the app queues the alert in AsyncStorage and sends it through FCM when the connection is back.
They're local notifications scheduled on the device, so they don't need the internet.

answers.why: Long but vague; right idea without mechanism.
answers.answer: This was something we thought about a lot because elderly users often have bad connectivity or turn off their data to save money. We wanted the app to be reliable no matter what, so we made sure the reminders work even without internet, and we tested it by turning on airplane mode on a few different phones and it worked well in our testing. The caregivers also get alerts in some cases.

answers.why: False: FCM requires network; local notifications don't route through Firebase servers.
answers.answer: Firebase Cloud Messaging keeps a copy of every reminder on the phone and delivers it from Google's servers even when the phone is offline, so that's what guarantees the reminder fires.
Offline support is important for mobile apps. Apps should store data locally and sync when the network becomes available.

items.question: How did LibSearch handle misspelled book titles?

answers.why: Correct Elasticsearch fuzziness mechanism, a tuning decision with reason.
answers.answer: The title field uses a match query with fuzziness set to AUTO, so Elasticsearch allows one or two character edits depending on word length. Short words stay exact, otherwise 'cat' matched everything. I also kept a prefix length of 1, because students rarely get the first letter wrong and it made queries a lot faster.
Fuzzy matching in Elasticsearch, fuzziness AUTO on the title field.
Elasticsearch has some built-in way to handle typos so we used that, it worked most of the time.

answers.why: Wrong: Levenshtein fuzziness is edit distance, not phonetic, and isn't unlimited.
answers.answer: We used fuzziness, which works by converting each word into how it sounds, so any spelling that sounds the same will match, with no limit on how many letters are wrong. That's why it can find any title even if every letter is wrong.
Elasticsearch, Flask, React, fuzzy matching, author boosting, full-text search, relevance ranking, 40,000 records.
The librarians really liked the new UI, they said it was much faster than the old system they had.

items.question: Why did you use WebSockets instead of plain HTTP requests for the GPS updates in FleetWatch?

answers.why: Correct trade-off, numbers, the cost they accepted and how they handled it.
answers.answer: Thirty phones sending a point every 10 seconds is fine either way; the real reason was pushing positions out to the dispatch map instantly without the browser polling. One WebSocket per phone avoids a new HTTPS handshake every 10 seconds, which mattered on bad mobile networks. The downside is connections drop constantly on the road, so the phone buffers points and resends them with their original timestamps after reconnecting, and the server ignores duplicates.
Persistent connections push updates to the dispatch map in real time and avoid reconnecting every 10 seconds on flaky mobile networks.

answers.why: Long but mostly generic about real-time; one relevant point.
answers.answer: Real-time was really important for the client because dispatchers need to know where vans are at all times. WebSockets are the modern way of building real-time features and a lot of big companies use them, and they felt more appropriate than normal HTTP requests. It also made the map on the dashboard update smoothly without refreshing, which the dispatchers liked a lot.

answers.why: False: WebSockets don't use UDP and don't guarantee delivery when the connection drops.
answers.answer: WebSockets run over UDP, so they are faster than HTTP, and they guarantee that no GPS point is ever lost even if the phone loses signal, because the protocol stores undelivered messages on the server.
HTTP is a request-response protocol, while WebSockets provide full-duplex communication over a single TCP connection. WebSockets are typically used for chat applications, games and live dashboards.
it was in the requirements

items.question: During your internship at ExamPro, how did you deal with flaky end-to-end tests?

answers.answer: Most failures were timing: tests clicked Submit before the answer had autosaved, so it passed locally and failed in CI where the runner was slower. I replaced the fixed sleeps with explicit waits on the 'Saved' indicator, and gave each test its own exam session through an API fixture instead of sharing one. Over the next two weeks the suite went from failing about one run in four to almost never.
Swapped sleeps for explicit waits on the autosave indicator and gave each test its own exam session.
I added retries for the tests that failed randomly so the pipeline stayed green. I know that's more hiding the problem than fixing it, but we didn't have time to dig into each one.

answers.why: Wrong: Selenium implicit waits don't make tests deterministic and time.sleep everywhere makes flakiness worse; claim of zero flakiness is unsupported.
answers.answer: I added time.sleep(10) after every single step, which is the recommended Selenium practice and completely eliminates flaky tests, so after that we never had a single failure.
Flaky tests are a common problem in software testing. Good practices include isolating tests, avoiding shared state, and making tests deterministic so the results can be trusted.
The internship was remote so I mostly talked to my manager on Slack, the team was really friendly.

items.question: Why did you use transfer learning on MobileNetV2 instead of training a model from scratch?

answers.why: Correct reasons (data size, pretrained features, mobile constraints), a concrete process detail and result.
answers.answer: We only had about 9,000 labelled leaf photos, which isn't enough to train a CNN from scratch without heavy overfitting. MobileNetV2 already knows edges and textures from ImageNet, so I froze the base, trained a new 12-class head, then unfroze the top 30 layers with a low learning rate. It was also chosen because it's small and fast enough for TensorFlow Lite on cheap Android phones — around 100 ms per photo.
Not enough data to train from scratch, and MobileNetV2 is small enough to run on phones with TFLite.
Training from scratch takes a lot of time, transfer learning is faster and gives good accuracy.

answers.why: False: MobileNetV2 wasn't trained on plant diseases; ImageNet weights don't include these classes.
answers.answer: MobileNetV2 was already trained by Google on tomato leaf diseases, so it already knew all 12 diseases and we didn't really need to train anything, just load it.

answers.why: Long textbook explanation, nothing about their project.
answers.answer: Transfer learning is a machine learning technique where a model developed for one task is reused as the starting point for a model on a second task. It is very popular in deep learning because pre-trained models on large datasets like ImageNet have already learned useful features. This approach can save a lot of computational resources and time, and it often leads to better performance, especially when the target dataset is small. Many applications in computer vision use transfer learning today.

items.question: What did you personally build in SplitLedger?

answers.why: Clear personal ownership, specific design decision with reason, honest about team.
answers.answer: I wrote the settle-up logic. It nets everyone's balances and then repeatedly matches the person who owes the most with the person who's owed the most, so a group of four never needs more than three payments. Amounts are stored as integer paise in MySQL, not floats, after we saw rounding errors of a rupee in testing. The PDF statements and the frontend were my teammates'.
The settle-up algorithm — net balances, then match largest debtor with largest creditor — and storing money as integer paise.

I was involved in quite a lot of the project honestly, we all worked together and helped each other whenever someone was stuck. I did some backend work with Node and Express and a bit of the database side, and I also helped with testing and the presentation at the end. It was a great learning experience for teamwork.

answers.why: Contradicts team of four with an implausible solo claim.
answers.answer: I built everything myself, the backend, the database, the PDFs and the frontend. The other three just tested it.
Node.js, Express, MySQL, settle-up, transactions, PDF statements, REST API, hostel expenses.

items.question: How did you stop HelpBot from giving wrong answers when the help articles didn't cover a question?

answers.why: Concrete threshold mechanism, prompt constraint, measurement.
answers.answer: If the best FAISS match had a cosine similarity below 0.45, the bot skipped the LLM entirely and replied that it didn't know, with a link to raise a ticket. Above that, the prompt only allows answering from the retrieved articles and every answer cites them. I tuned the 0.45 on 80 real helpdesk questions, about a third of which weren't covered by any article.
A similarity threshold on the top retrieved article — below it the bot says it doesn't know instead of calling the LLM.
Mostly by telling the model in the prompt to only use the articles. It still made things up sometimes, I didn't fully solve that.

answers.why: False: RAG does not guarantee answers are correct; Llama 3 can still hallucinate with retrieved context.
answers.answer: RAG solves that by itself, because once the model has retrieved documents it is mathematically impossible for it to hallucinate, so we didn't need anything else.

answers.why: Long generic explanation of hallucination, nothing specific.
answers.answer: Hallucination is one of the biggest challenges with large language models today. LLMs generate text based on patterns they learned during training, so they can sometimes produce information that sounds plausible but is incorrect. Researchers are working on many techniques to reduce hallucination, such as retrieval-augmented generation, better training data and human feedback. It is important for developers to be aware of this limitation when building chatbots.
FAISS, sentence-transformers, Llama 3, RAG, retrieval, embeddings, source links, 300 articles.
